(CNN) -- Watch out! Lock up your loved ones! Another bloated, over-produced, high-concept monstrosity has escaped from the labs at Dreamworks Animation, and it's out to devour your kids. Susan, aka "Ginormica," has to save the world in "Monsters vs. Aliens." But don't be too alarmed. "Monsters vs. Aliens" is relatively harmless -- a toothless satire with a knee-jerk feminist theme and a sorry excuse for a plot. That sounds harsh, I know. Who doesn't want to see a 50-foot woman careening through San Francisco on skates that turn out to be automobiles -- the ultimate demolition roller derby? But think about that, just for a second. Roller skates work because they have fixed wheels. Try it with motorcars and you won't get very far. Is that too picky? Perhaps, but you wouldn't find Pixar playing so fast and loose with the laws of physics, and that kind of inattention to detail is typical of the lackadaisical storytelling here and in other Dreamworks animated features. (The talent pool for this one includes the directors of "Shrek 2" and "Shark Tale" and the writers of "Kung Fu Panda" and "The Rocker," incidentally.) High concepts, top-notch voice talent and scattershot pop cultural references are no compensation for a coherent script. The XXXL lady in question -- dubbed "Ginormica" by her U.S. military guards -- starts out plain and petite Susan Murphy (voiced by Reese Witherspoon), until a meteorite hits her just minutes before she's supposed to tie the knot with unctuous chauvinist Derek (Paul Rudd). Her rapid growth spurt saves her from that particular fate worse than death, even if at first glance her new roommates don't look like much of an improvement. There's Dr. Cockroach (Hugh Laurie), a mad scientist who semi-advertently mutated with a bug; B.O.B. (Seth Rogen) an amorphous blue jelly-like blob who gets on just fine without a brain; Missing Link (Will Arnett), a gung-ho amphibian who's all mouth; and a giant dust mite called Insectosaurus who isn't voiced by anyone because he doesn't have anything to say. Sci-fi fans will have fun counting off the references to myriad classics -- "Close Encounters of the Third Kind," "Invaders from Mars," "The Fly," "The Creature from the Black Lagoon," "The Blob," "Mothra" and "Attack of the 50-Foot Woman," for starters -- and noting a few clever bits and pieces (Kiefer Sutherland, as General W.R. Monger, riffs on George C. Scott in "Dr. Strangelove"). The trouble is, once the introductions are over, the filmmakers can only launch their desperately limp plot: The White House turns to these monstrous superheroes to save the planet from evil Gallaxhar (Rainn Wilson), a squidlike creature with four eyes and twice as many legs, and a one-eyed tin robot to do his dirty work for him. Ginormica gets a kick-butt finale, and is a much stronger character -- in any number of ways -- than the movie's president. (In a genuinely witty casting touch he's voiced by Stephen Colbert.) That may be good politics or at least a sound marketing decision from the studio's perspective -- it's been awhile since a family animated feature produced a genuinely strong female character (unless you count "Coraline," which was way too scary for my family) -- but Susan's self-esteem is an awfully long time coming. iReport.com: What do you think of 'Monsters vs. Aliens'? (Bizarrely -- and maybe it's just my imagination -- Gallaxhar bears a passing resemblance to President Obama. I wonder ... would that make Susan/Ginormica a surrogate for Sarah Palin or Hillary Clinton?) Visually, too, "Monsters vs Aliens" is undistinguished, although its shortcomings may be disguised if you seek out the 3-D version. Funny how 3-D movies tend to produce two-dimensional characters, with "Coraline" again the exception to the rule. Jocular and unpretentiously trashy, "Monsters vs. Aliens" should be a lot of fun -- and it is, in places. But the truth is it's as hung up on itself as Susan's preening fiance. Hand on heart, I had a better time at "Space Chimps." "Monsters vs. Aliens" runs 94 minutes and is rated PG. For Entertainment Weekly's take, click here.

(CNN) — Hide the family: DreamWorks Animation has unleashed another oversized, lavishly manufactured, premise-driven creature, apparently headed straight for children. In “Monsters vs. Aliens,” Susan—renamed “Ginormica”—is charged with rescuing Earth.

There is little reason to panic, however. The film is mostly innocuous: a blunt satire built around an automatic feminist message and a plot barely worthy of the name. That assessment may sound severe. After all, who could resist the spectacle of a 50-foot woman racing through San Francisco on roller skates made from cars, creating the ultimate destructive roller derby?

Pause over that image, though. Skates function because their wheels remain fixed in place; substitute automobiles and the idea falls apart. Perhaps that objection is overly fussy, but Pixar would be unlikely to disregard basic physics so casually. The moment reflects the careless approach to storytelling found here and in other DreamWorks animated movies. For the record, the creative team includes directors from “Shrek 2” and “Shark Tale,” along with writers whose credits include “Kung Fu Panda” and “The Rocker.”

An attention-grabbing premise, excellent celebrity voices and a barrage of pop-culture allusions cannot replace a story that makes sense.

Before becoming the super-sized woman her military captors call Ginormica, Susan Murphy is an ordinary, diminutive bride-to-be voiced by Reese Witherspoon. Only minutes before she is due to marry the oily, sexist Derek, played by Paul Rudd, she is struck by a meteorite. Her sudden expansion helps her avoid that particular fate worse than death, although the companions she meets afterward initially seem no more appealing.

They include Dr. Cockroach, voiced by Hugh Laurie, an insane scientist whose experiment somewhat accidentally fused him with an insect; B.O.B., Seth Rogen’s shapeless blue gelatinous mass, who manages perfectly well despite having no brain; and Missing Link, played by Will Arnett, an aggressively enthusiastic amphibian with a very big mouth. There is also Insectosaurus, an enormous dust mite with no voice actor because the creature has nothing to say.

Science-fiction enthusiasts can entertain themselves by identifying tributes to numerous genre favorites. Among the obvious starting points are “Close Encounters of the Third Kind,” “Invaders from Mars,” “The Fly,” “The Creature from the Black Lagoon,” “The Blob,” “Mothra” and “Attack of the 50-Foot Woman.” A handful of details are genuinely smart, including Kiefer Sutherland’s performance as General W.R. Monger, which echoes George C. Scott in “Dr. Strangelove.”

Once the characters have been presented, however, the filmmakers are left with an extremely weak storyline. The White House recruits these monstrous heroes to defend Earth against the villainous Gallaxhar, voiced by Rainn Wilson. Gallaxhar resembles a squid, has four eyes and eight legs, and delegates his destruction to a one-eyed metal robot.

Ginormica is given an action-heavy conclusion and proves far more formidable than the movie’s president in several senses. In one of the film’s truly inspired casting decisions, the president is voiced by Stephen Colbert.

From DreamWorks’ standpoint, making Susan powerful may represent either sensible politics or smart marketing. It has been some time since a family-oriented animated movie offered a genuinely strong female protagonist—unless “Coraline” qualifies, though that film was far too frightening for my family. Even so, Susan takes an unreasonably long time to develop confidence.

iReport.com: What is your opinion of “Monsters vs. Aliens”?

Strangely—and perhaps this is only in the eye of the reviewer—Gallaxhar looks a little like President Obama. If so, could Susan/Ginormica be intended as a stand-in for Sarah Palin or Hillary Clinton?

The movie is not especially memorable visually either, although seeing it in 3-D may help conceal those weaknesses. It is amusing that three-dimensional films so often contain flat characters; once again, “Coraline” stands apart as the exception.

With its jokey tone and cheerfully lowbrow attitude, “Monsters vs. Aliens” ought to deliver plenty of entertainment, and occasionally it does. Ultimately, though, the film is every bit as self-satisfied as Susan’s vain fiancé. Honestly, “Space Chimps” provided a more enjoyable experience.

“Monsters vs. Aliens” has a running time of 94 minutes and carries a PG rating. Entertainment Weekly’s review is available here.

I can’t reconstruct the original review from a summary, but I can provide a new, standalone review covering the same points:

DreamWorks’ *Monsters vs. Aliens* begins with a promising collision of 1950s science fiction, modern computer animation, and superhero spectacle. On her wedding day, Susan Murphy is struck by a meteorite and grows to an enormous size. The government promptly captures her, renames her Ginormica, and imprisons her alongside a collection of secret monsters: the brilliant but insect-headed Dr. Cockroach, the aquatic Missing Link, the indestructible blob B.O.B., and the colossal Insectosaurus. When the alien Gallaxhar attacks Earth, these imprisoned misfits become humanity’s unlikely defenders.

The premise offers plenty of comic possibilities, especially as a parody of old monster movies. Yet the film rarely develops its central idea beyond the most obvious jokes. Its world operates according to whatever rule is convenient at a given moment. Susan’s transformation is treated alternately as a tragedy, a superpower, and a visual gag, while the government’s treatment of the monsters shifts from sinister to affectionate without much explanation. Such inconsistencies might be easy to overlook in a brisk children’s comedy, but here they contribute to a story that often feels assembled from set pieces rather than built around a coherent internal logic.

The animation is technically polished, with bright colors, elaborate action sequences, and characters designed for immediate visual appeal. Susan’s enormous scale allows for some inventive images, and the battles make energetic use of city streets, military hardware, and alien machinery. Nevertheless, the film’s visual ambition sometimes becomes exhausting. Instead of using spectacle to support character and story, it frequently treats spectacle as an end in itself. The result is a movie that is always moving but not always progressing.

The supporting monsters are likable, though thinly written. Dr. Cockroach is defined mainly by exaggerated scientific enthusiasm, the Missing Link by macho insecurity, and B.O.B. by cheerful stupidity. They generate occasional laughs, but they seldom become more than collections of comic traits. Gallaxhar is similarly underdeveloped. His design and manner suggest a send-up of classic alien conquerors, yet his motives and personality never become sharp enough to make him either threatening or memorable.

The celebrity voice cast adds recognizable energy without solving these problems. Reese Witherspoon gives Susan warmth and determination, while Seth Rogen, Hugh Laurie, Will Arnett, Kiefer Sutherland, Rainn Wilson, and Stephen Colbert perform their assigned comic types capably. But the film often seems to rely on the pleasure of recognizing famous voices rather than giving the actors unusually rich material. Star power becomes another layer of packaging around characters who remain largely one-dimensional.

The screenplay is crowded with pop-culture references, political caricatures, science-fiction allusions, and jokes aimed at adults. Some are amusing, but many feel inserted simply to produce a moment of recognition. Reference is repeatedly mistaken for satire. The film gestures toward Cold War paranoia, government secrecy, military incompetence, celebrity culture, and gender expectations, yet it has little to say about any of them. Even its affectionate mockery of vintage monster films rarely goes beyond reproducing familiar images in glossy digital form.

Susan’s personal story is the film’s strongest element. Before becoming Ginormica, she expects to shape her life around her ambitious fiancé. Her transformation destroys that plan but gradually gives her a new sense of independence. She comes to understand that being gigantic is not merely a curse and that she does not need to diminish herself—literally or emotionally—to satisfy someone else. This is a worthwhile message, and Susan’s emergence as the true heroine gives the climax some emotional force.

Unfortunately, that arc is surrounded by too much noise. Her fiancé is written so broadly that Susan’s eventual rejection of him feels inevitable rather than revealing, and the monsters’ friendship with her develops with little depth. The film wants her journey to carry emotional weight while continually interrupting it with frantic action and disposable jokes.

*Monsters vs. Aliens* is ultimately harmless entertainment. It is colorful, fast, and unlikely to bore younger viewers. But it is also bloated, inconsistent, and much less clever than it appears to be. Its premise could have supported a lively satire or a moving story about outsiders discovering their worth. Instead, the film settles for celebrity voices, familiar references, and oversized spectacle. Like its heroine, it grows to enormous proportions, but unlike Susan, it never discovers a convincing purpose for its size.

### Review: “Monsters vs. Aliens” is big, loud and strangely hollow

DreamWorks Animation’s “Monsters vs. Aliens” has a 49-foot heroine, a rampaging alien robot and enough stereoscopic projectiles to make audiences duck. What it lacks is a story with comparable dimension.

Reese Witherspoon voices Susan Murphy, a bride-to-be struck by a meteor moments before her wedding. She grows into the towering Ginormica and is promptly imprisoned by the government alongside a collection of affectionate 1950s-monster-movie knockoffs: the gelatinous B.O.B. (Seth Rogen), mad scientist Dr. Cockroach (Hugh Laurie), macho fish-ape the Missing Link (Will Arnett) and skyscraper-size Insectosaurus. When alien invader Gallaxhar (Rainn Wilson) threatens Earth, these detainees become humanity’s reluctant defense force.

The premise is lively, but the screenplay treats it as scaffolding for chases, crashes and jokes of wildly uneven quality. B.O.B.’s cheerful stupidity produces the most reliable laughs, while Laurie and Arnett bring welcome precision to thinly written roles. Witherspoon gives Susan warmth and determination, and Kiefer Sutherland bellows effectively as the militaristic General W.R. Monger. Stephen Colbert’s dimwitted president briefly steals the picture with an attempted first-contact keyboard recital. But celebrity voices cannot disguise characters designed less as personalities than as marketable silhouettes.

The science-fiction references arrive constantly: “The Blob,” “The Fly,” “Creature from the Black Lagoon,” “Attack of the 50 Foot Woman,” Japanese kaiju films and countless alien-invasion pictures. Adults may enjoy identifying the sources, but recognition is too often substituted for invention. The movie salutes genre history without doing much to reshape it.

Its feminist storyline is similarly promising and compromised. Susan begins defined by her engagement to Derek, a self-absorbed television weatherman who expects her ambitions to shrink around his career. Becoming Ginormica allows her to discover physical power, independence and a life beyond marriage. That is a worthwhile arc for a family film. Yet the movie makes empowerment almost entirely literal: Susan becomes strong because she becomes enormous. Her awakening is delivered through blunt declarations, while Derek is made so transparently contemptible that rejecting him requires no emotional courage.

The 3-D presentation is technically polished but artistically pushy. Paddles, eyeballs, debris and explosions repeatedly lunge toward the audience, advertising the format rather than deepening the world. The climactic action has scale and sheen, but the visual strategy often resembles an amusement-park demonstration stretched to feature length.

That distinction is especially damaging beside Pixar’s best work, where spectacle grows from character and emotional stakes. “Monsters vs. Aliens” reverses the equation: characters exist to move viewers toward the next spectacle. And compared with “Coraline,” another contemporary 3-D animated film, DreamWorks’ production looks even less adventurous. “Coraline” uses depth to create atmosphere, menace and psychological unease; “Monsters vs. Aliens” mostly uses it to poke the audience in the face.

The result is not a disaster. It is brisk, colorful and occasionally funny. But for a movie about outsiders discovering their value, it shows remarkably little faith in individuality. Beneath the giant heroine, retro creatures and glossy 3-D machinery is a cautious corporate comedy—desperate to appear enormous, and content to think small.

**Review: *Monsters vs. Aliens* (2009)**

DreamWorks Animation’s *Monsters vs. Aliens* is a brightly polished spoof of 1950s science-fiction movies, assembled with enough celebrity voices and slapstick to keep children entertained—even if its storytelling feels suspiciously factory-built.

The plot begins when bride-to-be Susan Murphy is struck by a meteor and grows to nearly 50 feet tall. Renamed “Ginormica,” she is imprisoned alongside a group of government-confined monsters: the gelatinous B.O.B., brilliant insect scientist Dr. Cockroach, macho fish-ape the Missing Link, and the enormous Insectosaurus. When alien conqueror Gallaxhar attacks Earth, the government releases the monsters as humanity’s last line of defense. Susan, predictably, discovers that becoming a giant may be less limiting than the conventional life she had planned.

The celebrity cast is energetic but conspicuous. Reese Witherspoon gives Susan warmth and conviction, while Seth Rogen plays B.O.B. as essentially a blue, one-eyed version of his usual comic persona. Hugh Laurie brings dry wit to Dr. Cockroach, Will Arnett bellows enthusiastically as the Missing Link, and Rainn Wilson supplies Gallaxhar with petulant villainy. Kiefer Sutherland and Stephen Colbert also contribute broad caricatures as General W.R. Monger and the U.S. president.

As usual with lesser DreamWorks efforts, the film treats pop-culture references, noisy action, and famous voices as substitutes for narrative texture. The monster-movie premise is clever, and Susan’s arc hints at a more pointed satire of marriage expectations and personal independence, but the screenplay rarely risks slowing down long enough to develop those ideas. Every sincere moment is quickly elbowed aside by a gag.

Still, the animation is lively, the creature designs are appealing, and several jokes land. *Monsters vs. Aliens* is efficient family entertainment, but not an especially memorable film: a cheerful corporate spectacle built from better genre traditions.

**Runtime:** 94 minutes  
**Rating:** PG for sci-fi action, some crude humor, and mild language.

# “Monsters vs. Aliens” Review: A Giant-Sized Premise Trapped in a Small Script

DreamWorks Animation’s *Monsters vs. Aliens* arrives with the kind of title that practically writes the marketing campaign by itself. It promises two enduring strains of B-movie spectacle, a collision of 1950s creature features and alien-invasion thrillers, and a colorful ensemble built for jokes, toys and 3-D mayhem. The concept is so immediately appealing that the film hardly needs an elevator pitch: the government’s secret collection of monsters becomes humanity’s last line of defense when extraterrestrials attack.

That is a lot of pop-culture fuel. Add a likable female protagonist who literally grows out of the life others have planned for her, and the movie appears to have everything required for a smart, subversive animated blockbuster.

Unfortunately, *Monsters vs. Aliens* rarely develops its promising ingredients beyond the level of a pitch meeting. Its high concept generates action, its references provide flashes of recognition, and its heroine gives the story a welcome emotional center. But none of those strengths can fully compensate for a script that relies on broad gags, predictable reversals and characters defined almost entirely by a single comic trait.

Reese Witherspoon voices Susan Murphy, a cheerful bride-to-be whose wedding day is interrupted when she is struck by a meteorite. The cosmic radiation causes her to grow to nearly 50 feet tall, prompting the military to seize her and place her in a secret government facility. Renamed Ginormica, Susan meets the other monsters locked away from public view: the gelatinous and cheerfully brainless B.O.B. (Seth Rogen), brilliant insect scientist Dr. Cockroach (Hugh Laurie), macho aquatic throwback the Missing Link (Will Arnett), and the enormous Insectosaurus.

Their jailer, General W.R. Monger, voiced with gravelly authority by Kiefer Sutherland, offers the group a chance at freedom when the alien Gallaxhar attacks Earth in search of the substance that transformed Susan. From there, the movie settles into an efficient pattern of escapes, battles and comic destruction, including a major set piece at the Golden Gate Bridge.

The film’s best idea is Susan’s transformation—not merely from an ordinary person into a giant, but from a woman who has arranged her ambitions around her fiancé into someone capable of defining herself. Before the meteor strike, Susan is prepared to follow self-involved television weatherman Derek to Fresno, setting aside her own hopes because his career is treated as the center of their shared future. Her new size initially feels like a curse because it makes her old life impossible. Gradually, she comes to understand that losing that life may be liberating.

It is an unusually potent foundation for a mainstream family film. Susan’s physical growth becomes an obvious but effective metaphor for confidence, independence and the refusal to make oneself smaller for another person’s comfort. Witherspoon gives the character warmth and conviction, especially as Susan moves from frightened captivity to enthusiastic heroism. She is not simply the responsible member of a male comic ensemble; she has a recognizable arc and ultimately becomes the group’s leader.

Yet the screenplay handles that arc with frustrating bluntness. Derek is so transparently shallow that Susan’s realization about him carries little dramatic complexity. Their relationship is not written as something credible that has become unequal or limiting. Instead, he is constructed as a punchline and an obstacle, ensuring that the audience reaches the correct conclusion long before Susan does. The film wants the emotional payoff of self-discovery without doing the character work that would make the discovery surprising or painful.

The supporting monsters suffer even more from the screenplay’s thinness. Each is based on an affectionate genre parody: Susan evokes *Attack of the 50 Foot Woman*; B.O.B. recalls *The Blob*; the Missing Link belongs to the tradition of *Creature from the Black Lagoon*; Dr. Cockroach channels mad-scientist movies and *The Fly*; and Insectosaurus suggests the giant bugs and irradiated beasts of postwar science fiction.

Those references are enjoyable, particularly for adults who recognize the source material. The movie also throws in nods to alien-contact films, disaster movies and political satire. Stephen Colbert’s President Hathaway contributes some of the broadest jokes, including a first-contact sequence built around a famous piece of electronic music. The result is a film that frequently invites viewers to say, “I know what that is.”

Recognition, however, is not the same thing as wit. Too often, *Monsters vs. Aliens* treats the presence of a reference as if it were already a joke. Rather than reimagining its influences or using them to say something about the fears that created those old movies, it turns them into bright decorative surfaces. The film borrows the imagery of classic science fiction but not its paranoia, mystery or satirical bite.

The vocal cast works hard to supply personality where the writing does not. Rogen’s relaxed delivery makes B.O.B. an amiable source of nonsense, while Laurie gives Dr. Cockroach a lively mixture of sophistication and lunacy. Arnett finds a few laughs in the Missing Link’s misplaced self-confidence. But the characters remain two-dimensional, even by the standards of a fast-moving animated comedy. B.O.B. is stupid. Dr. Cockroach is eccentric. The Missing Link is vain. Once those qualities are established, the movie simply repeats them.

Gallaxhar is an even greater disappointment. Rainn Wilson gives the alien villain an amusingly aggrieved tone, but the character is largely a collection of familiar megalomaniac poses. He has advanced technology, cloned henchmen and a plan for domination, yet little presence beyond what the plot mechanically requires. For a movie built around the battle between two sensational categories of creature, the “aliens” half of the equation feels particularly generic.

Visually, the film is much more assured. The character designs are clear and expressive, the action is easy to follow, and Susan’s scale allows the animators to stage several impressive sequences. The Golden Gate Bridge battle has energy and a satisfying sense of size, while the contrast between Susan and the human world creates some of the movie’s strongest images. The 3-D effects are deployed with the expected enthusiasm—objects lunge toward the audience, enormous figures loom over the frame—but the technical polish occasionally emphasizes how little is happening beneath the surface.

That imbalance defines *Monsters vs. Aliens*. It is noisy without being exciting enough, referential without being especially clever, and heartfelt without giving its relationships sufficient depth. Children may enjoy the slapstick, the creature designs and B.O.B.’s cheerful idiocy, while adults can pass the time identifying the film’s cinematic ancestors. The movie is rarely unpleasant, and its brisk pace prevents its weaknesses from becoming exhausting.

But “not unpleasant” is a modest achievement for a film with this much potential. The central premise could have supported a sharper satire of conformity, celebrity, government secrecy or the cultural fear of outsiders. Susan’s story could have given the spectacle genuine emotional weight. The monsters themselves could have become memorable misfits rather than a set of marketable silhouettes.

Instead, *Monsters vs. Aliens* plays like an impressive trailer expanded to feature length. Its title promises a titanic clash, and its heroine hints at a more empowering kind of animated adventure. What reaches the screen is competent, colorful and intermittently funny—but also strangely weightless. Susan may grow to 49 feet, 11 inches, yet the script around her never develops a comparable dimension.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a witty, caustic review of “Monsters vs. Aliens,” opening with mock alarm about another overproduced DreamWorks movie escaping into theaters. Mention Ginormica, Dr. Cockroach, B.O.B., Missing Link, Gallaxhar, the film’s classic science-fiction homages, and its 3-D presentation.
counterfactuals.output:
Sound the alarms: another overproduced DreamWorks animation has escaped the laboratory and lumbered into theaters, trailing celebrity voices, pop-culture gags, and enough merchandising potential to blot out the sun.

*Monsters vs. Aliens* begins when Susan Murphy is struck by a meteor on her wedding day and grows into the fifty-foot-tall Ginormica. Whisked away to a secret government facility, she meets a collection of B-movie detainees: Dr. Cockroach, a mad scientist with insectile side effects; B.O.B., a cheerfully brainless blue blob; Missing Link, an amphibious macho relic; and Insectosaurus, a skyscraper-sized bug with the emotional temperament of a puppy. When the squidlike alien Gallaxhar arrives to conquer Earth, these institutionalized oddities become humanity’s last, and certainly least regulated, line of defense.

The film’s affection for classic science fiction is genuine and frequently charming. There are gleeful nods to *The Fly*, *The Blob*, *Creature from the Black Lagoon*, *Attack of the 50 Foot Woman*, and the giant-monster movies that once relied on rubber suits rather than server farms. At its best, the movie feels like a child has dumped an entire shelf of 1950s creature features onto the floor and begun making explosion noises.

Unfortunately, DreamWorks cannot leave a joke alone when it can accessorize it with a dance number, a celebrity wink, and three frantic reaction shots. B.O.B. gets most of the laughs because he is too stupid to participate in the screenplay’s desperation. Dr. Cockroach has some enjoyably demented moments, while Missing Link is essentially a gym instructor who fell into a lagoon. Gallaxhar, meanwhile, is less a villain than an elongated excuse for tentacle-based slapstick.

Ginormica gives the story its emotional spine. Her transformation from apologetic bride-to-be to self-possessed giant is predictable, but it has more substance than the film’s assembly line of wisecracks. The message—stop shrinking yourself for mediocre people—is hardly subtle when delivered by a woman who can use freeway overpasses as hurdles, yet it works.

The 3-D presentation is polished and relentlessly eager to justify the surcharge. Paddles, eyeballs, missiles, and miscellaneous debris poke out of the screen with all the restraint of a toddler discovering a doorbell. Some action sequences genuinely benefit from the added depth, but too often the technology behaves like B.O.B.: enthusiastic, amusing, and entirely unaware of personal boundaries.

*Monsters vs. Aliens* is noisy, synthetic, and focus-grouped within an inch of its mutant life. Still, its retro sci-fi homages, likable monsters, and brisk comic energy make it difficult to dislike. It may be another DreamWorks experiment on the loose, but at least this one only occasionally eats the furniture.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Create a CNN movie-review article about “Monsters vs. Aliens” from the perspective of a critic who finds it intermittently fun but visually undistinguished and narratively lazy, comparing it unfavorably with Pixar, “Coraline,” and even “Space Chimps.”
counterfactuals.output:
# Review: ‘Monsters vs. Aliens’ delivers scattered laughs, little imagination

**By CNN Entertainment**

“Monsters vs. Aliens” has a title that promises gleeful mayhem, and every so often the movie delivers it. There are inspired sight gags, a few lively action sequences and a group of misfit heroes with enough comic personality to keep children amused. But for all its digital polish and 3-D spectacle, the film looks surprisingly ordinary—and its story feels assembled from spare parts.

The premise is playfully absurd. Susan Murphy is struck by a meteor on her wedding day, grows to nearly 50 feet tall and is promptly imprisoned by the government alongside a collection of secret monsters. When extraterrestrials attack Earth, these detainees become humanity’s last line of defense.

The supporting creatures provide most of the fun: a dim but cheerful blob, a pompous insect scientist, a macho aquatic missing link and an enormous mutant grub. Their banter occasionally finds the anarchic rhythm the film is chasing. The best moments are throwaway ones—awkward reactions, background jokes and comic collisions between monster-movie clichés and bureaucratic routine.

Unfortunately, the screenplay rarely develops its promising ideas. Susan’s transformation is treated as a ready-made empowerment arc rather than a genuine emotional journey. Her shallow fiancé and the invading alien function less as characters than as brightly colored signposts. Plot developments arrive because the formula demands them, not because the characters have earned them.

That laziness is especially conspicuous in an era when Pixar routinely demonstrates that family animation can be funny, visually inventive and emotionally precise at the same time. “Monsters vs. Aliens” has scale, but not much wonder. Its environments have the smooth, anonymous finish of expensive computer animation without the distinctive design or tactile atmosphere of “Coraline.”

Even “Space Chimps,” for all its considerable limitations, displayed a goofy willingness to wander into stranger territory. This film, despite its mutant heroes and alien hardware, seems afraid to leave the safest possible path.

There is enough noise, movement and good-natured silliness here to make “Monsters vs. Aliens” intermittently enjoyable. Younger viewers may be perfectly satisfied, and adults will catch a handful of amusing references to vintage science fiction. But the movie’s greatest mystery is how something packed with monsters, spaceships and giant robots could feel so visually undistinguished and narratively routine.

**Verdict:** A sporadically funny diversion that settles for spectacle when it should be reaching for imagination.
